title: How Smart Are 'Water Smart Landscapes'?
publisher: arXiv preprint (econ.EM) 1803.04593; later Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
finding: "We find an annual water bill savings of 79 cents per m2 of turf converted under WSL. Given a typical landscape conversion cost of $15/m2 ... this gives an unsubsidized and undiscounted repayment period of nineteen years." The program paid "between $0.50 and $2.00 per square foot of grass removed".
location: Section 6.4.2 Private Benefits (p.32); program description p.7
conversion: Rebate needed to induce removal ~$1.50/sq ft; average participant saved 48,600 gal/yr which at SNWA's 55 gal/sq ft/yr implies ~880 sq ft removed, so ~$1,300 one-time payment; annuitised at 5% over 20 years gives ~$105 per season. My own arithmetic, not in the paper.
strengthWhy: Directly measures the payment size at which households will give up a lawn (revealed preference), the same mechanism the assumption needs, but the paper reports rebate rates and bill savings, not a willingness-to-pay per season; the per-season figure is my conversion.
differencesFromUtah: Las Vegas is hotter and drier than the Wasatch Front, has far higher water prices and an aggressive long-running cash-for-grass culture; Utah lawns are larger and water is much cheaper, which would raise the payment needed.
verification: pdftotext of the fetched PDF, grep + read of Section 6.4.2 and p.7

title: How Smart Are 'Water Smart Landscapes'? (negative capitalisation of xeric yards)
finding: "the private savings on individual's water bills from turf removal were likely inadequate to have functioned as a strong inducement for homeowners to have undertaken these changes without explicit subsidization" and "xeric landscapes capitalize negatively relative to green yards".
conversion: qualitative only - establishes that the value households place on a green lawn exceeds the water-bill saving, i.e. a positive and non-trivial season_value
strengthWhy: Supports the sign and rough order of the assumption but gives no dollar-per-season number.
differencesFromUtah: Nevada real-estate and landscape norms; Utah has cheaper water so the same conclusion would hold more strongly.

title: Estimating the Size and Impact of the Ecological Restoration Economy
authors: Todd K. BenDor, T. William Lester, Avery Livengood, Adam Davis, Logan Yonavjak
finding: "restoration supports as many as 33 jobs per $1 million invested" and "this value spans a range between 6.8 and 39.7 based on location, geographic scale, and restoration type"; their own IMPLAN run: "This activity directly generates 126,111 jobs each year" on "$9.47 billion in economic output".
location: Introduction ('Our current understanding of the restoration economy'); Results, IMPLAN modeling; Table 2 Direct Effect row
conversion: 126,111 direct jobs / $9.4800 billion direct gross output = 13.3 direct jobs per $1M/yr. The cited literature range 6.8-39.7 brackets the model's 7.4, which sits at the bottom of that range.
strengthWhy: Same mechanism (habitat restoration spending to employment), national input-output estimate, directly in the assumption's unit after simple division; not Utah-specific and the 33/6.8-39.7 figures are the authors' citation of prior work rather than their own estimate.
differencesFromUtah: National average across restoration types; Utah's labour costs, contractor availability and the crop-transition and monitoring components of the model's spending mix differ from the surveyed restoration firms.

title: Certainty of Punishment versus Severity of Punishment: Enforcement of Environmental Protection Laws
place: United States (chemical manufacturing facilities, Clean Water Act NPDES)
finding: "We find that, when enforcement certainty and severity are high, both components effectively deter pollution, with certainty more effective. In contrast, certainty and severity increases prove counter-productive when certainty and severity are low."
location: Abstract, p.0; marginal-effect regions Table 6 / p.26; Conclusion p.24
conversion: No share-compliance number: the paper reports marginal effects on discharge ratios, not compliance shares. Supports the DIRECTION of the model's claim (certainty > severity) only in the high-enforcement regime.
strengthWhy: First systematic certainty-vs-severity test in environmental enforcement and the mechanism is the same trade-off the model asserts, but the regulated agents are chemical plants, not households, and the outcome is pollutant discharge, not restriction compliance.
differencesFromUtah: Firms with compliance staff and permits, not households; federal Clean Water Act enforcement, not municipal watering ordinances; no Utah or drought context.

title: Certainty of Punishment versus Severity of Punishment (counter-evidence / caveat)
finding: "Both marginal effects are counter-productive for nearly 70 % of the observations (Region 1). In all of these cases, the severity effect significantly dominates ... in only 30 % of these cases is the difference significant, in which case the certainty effect dominates the severity effect".
strengthWhy: Directly qualifies the model's headline claim: over most of the sample severity, not certainty, dominated. The claim 'citation frequency matters far more than fine size' is not unconditionally supported.

title: Salt Lake County Consumptive Use Methodology and 2023 Results
authors: Jordan Valley Water Conservancy District (reporting required by Utah SB119, 2023)
publisher: Jordan Valley Water Conservancy District / Utah Division of Water Rights
finding: Table 1: "Residential + Institutional + Other (Acre-Feet) 198,829"; "Residential + Institutional + Other Return Flow (Acre-Feet) 89,576"; "2023 Total Consumptive Use (GPCD) 100". Method: "total water use in Salt Lake County minus the total return flows as measured at county water reclamation facilities".
conversion: 89,576 / 198,829 = 45% of residential-sector diversion returns via reclamation facilities, so 55% is consumed. A gallon of average household use saved yields ~0.55 gallons of net new downstream flow once the forgone return flow is netted out. Outdoor-only savings would approach 1.0; the model's 0.25 is well below both.
strengthWhy: Exactly the right place, the right water-supply system and the right mechanism (measured return flow at the reclamation plants feeding the Jordan River to Great Salt Lake), in the assumption's own unit after one division.
differencesFromUtah: None - this IS Salt Lake County. Caveat: it is a sector-average return-flow ratio, not a marginal one, and it does not trace whether the saved water is legally protected all the way to the lake.
verification: pdftotext -layout of the fetched PDF; Table 1 read directly
